opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core problem is that Go has an enormous branching factor. On a 19x19 board you have something like 250 legal moves at a typical position, and the game runs for a couple hundred moves. If your rollout policy just picks uniformly among valid moves, the vast majority of those moves are terrible. No strong player would ever consider them. So when you do Monte Carlo rollouts with a uniform policy, you're estimating the value of a position under the assumption that both players play essentially randomly for the rest of the game. That's a very noisy and very biased signal. A position that's winning for a strong player might look like a coin flip under random play, and vice versa.

The way I think about it is that tree search is a way of spending compute to improve on your prior. If your prior is uniform, you're spreading that compute across a huge number of branches that don't matter, so you need an astronomical number of simulations before the statistics concentrate on the moves that are actually relevant. Classic MCTS programs before AlphaGo used things like UCT plus a lot of handcrafted heuristics and pattern libraries precisely because pure uniform sampling was hopeless at full board size.

What AlphaGo, and then AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero, really changed was replacing that uniform prior with a learned policy network, and replacing the noisy rollout with a learned value network. The policy network tells you which handful of moves are worth exploring, so the search becomes much narrower and deeper. The value network lets you truncate the search instead of playing to the end randomly. And then there's this beautiful bootstrapping loop: the search produces a better policy than the raw network, you distill the search results back into the network, and the next round of search starts from a stronger prior.

I think the broader lesson, and this is something I care about a lot coming from robotics, is that search and learning are complementary. Search without a good prior doesn't scale, because the space is too big. Learning without search can plateau, because you never get that amplification step. The interesting question for domains like robotics or language models is what the equivalent of the "valid move" set even is, and how you get a prior good enough that search becomes tractable. In Go you at least have a crisp rule set and a perfect simulator. In the real world you have neither, so the quality of your learned prior matters even more.

r001.rationale: It says a uniform prior spreads compute across many irrelevant branches, requiring an enormous number of simulations to focus on relevant moves.

r002.rationale: It contrasts uniform sampling with a learned policy prior, but does not compare the problem to importance sampling.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the naive version of Monte Carlo tree search is you pick a node, and then from that node you just play out random legal moves until the game ends, and you count up who won. And the problem is that uniform sampling over valid moves is an incredibly bad prior for Go. The branching factor is something like 250 at the start of the game, and the vast majority of those moves are terrible. So the rollouts you get are basically two drunk players stumbling around the board, and the win rate you estimate from that tells you very little about what would happen between two competent players from that position.

There are a couple of concrete failure modes. One is variance. You need an enormous number of rollouts before the signal rises above the noise, because each individual rollout is so uninformative. The second is bias, which is actually worse. There are positions in Go, especially around life-and-death problems, where there's exactly one correct sequence and everything else loses. Under uniform random play, the probability of finding that sequence in a rollout is vanishingly small, so the search systematically misjudges those positions. It'll think a group is dead when it's alive, or vice versa. And a strong opponent will exploit exactly those blind spots.

So the obvious fix, and this is really what AlphaGo did, is to replace the uniform prior with a learned one. You train a policy network on human games or on self-play so that the distribution you sample from already concentrates mass on plausible moves. Now the tree expands in directions that actually matter, and you can afford to go deeper instead of wider. And then the second move is to get rid of the rollouts entirely and replace them with a value network, because even a decent rollout policy is still a noisy estimator compared to a function that's been trained to directly predict the outcome.

The way I think about it more generally is that search and learning are complementary. Search is a way of spending compute at inference time to improve on your prior, but the quality of that improvement is bounded by how good the prior is. If your prior is uniform, you're asking search to do all the work, and in a space this large it just can't. The learned policy is what makes the search tractable, and the search is what makes the learned policy better than it was, and you iterate. That loop is the interesting part, and I think it generalizes well beyond Go.

r001.rationale: It says uniform sampling wastes rollouts on mostly terrible moves, requiring enormous sampling effort and preventing efficient search.

r002.rationale: It describes using a learned policy to concentrate sampling on plausible moves, but does not draw an analogy to importance sampling.

astra-6.text:
The problem is that almost all valid moves are bad. In Go, you might have a couple hundred legal moves at a position, but only a handful are worth thinking deeply about. If you distribute your search uniformly, you spend most of your compute exploring branches that a strong player would dismiss immediately. And that waste compounds with every level of the tree.

So you want a learned policy that tells you where to look. It doesn’t have to reliably pick the best move on its own; it just needs to concentrate your search on promising moves. Then search can do the more expensive work of distinguishing between them.

The catch is that your policy can also miss something. If it assigns almost no probability to a surprising but brilliant move, your search may never discover it. So there’s a balance between exploiting what your policy already knows and exploring enough to correct its mistakes. Uniform sampling gives you coverage in principle, but with a finite compute budget, that coverage can be extremely shallow.

r001.rationale: It says uniform search spends most compute exploring bad branches that a strong player would dismiss, wasting effort throughout the tree.

r002.rationale: It recommends concentrating search on promising moves, but does not compare uniform Go tree search to an importance sampling problem.

sol-6.1.text:
The problem is that being a valid move tells you very little about whether it’s a useful move. In Go, you can have hundreds of legal moves, but only a handful that a strong player would seriously consider. If you allocate your search budget uniformly, you spend almost all your compute exploring things that don’t matter.

And that compounds as you go deeper. Even if you sample a good first move, you need plausible responses from your opponent for the continuation to tell you anything. A move that works against random play might be terrible against a strong opponent.

So you want a learned policy to guide the search toward promising moves, and a value function to help evaluate positions without having to play everything out. You still need exploration, because your policy can be wrong. But the useful thing about search is that you can spend more computation resolving uncertainty among plausible alternatives, instead of treating every legal move as equally worth investigating.

r001.rationale: It explains that uniform allocation spends most computation exploring legal moves that do not matter, making search inefficient.

r002.rationale: It recommends guiding search toward promising moves, but does not compare uniform Go tree search to an importance sampling problem.
